transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-07
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Rajesh Iyer (Redwood SE), Noelle Tran (Redwood CSM), Marta Lopez (AperturePay Head of Platform), Noah Kim (AperturePay CTO), Daniel Price (AperturePay SRE), Priya Shah (AperturePay Security), Evan Green (Product)

Summary:
Short postmortem walkthrough for the token-throttle cascade on 2026-01-05. Focus: root causes (client-side retry storm + mis-sized KV cache), temporary mitigations we applied, and handoff of durable reliability fixes and security sign-offs.

Topics:
- Request distribution and long-tail throttling
- KV cache sizing and prefix cache misses
- Autoscale/governor knobs and rapid rollback strategy
- Compliance/KMS questions tied to private deployment path
- Next steps and owners

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we'll keep this tight, we have an hour. Rajesh and I will run through the incident timeline then hand to Marta and team for questions.
[00:34] Marta: Thanks Lena. Appreciate you prioritizing this. We had a big customer-facing outage Fri morning, about 18% error rate for 27 minutes, production traffic.
[01:12] Rajesh: Quick correction — the error spike was mostly 503s from our gateway due to token-throttle backpressure, and there was a correlated KV cache spike where cold prefixes blew out CPU on the worker pool.
[01:45] Noah: Just so I'm clear, is the KV thing on your side or ours? We saw a lot of misses when sequences hit 4k tokens.
[02:10] Rajesh: It's a mix. The model variant we were falling back to had a larger context and caused more KV inflation per request. Also your client retry policy amplified inflight requests — a retry storm pattern. Speech-to-text I keep mixing terms sorry, but the point is request fan-in exceeded the governor.
[02:46] Daniel: We did change a client-side timeout last week to be more aggressive, which I admit could be a contributor. But upstreaming a safe default shouldn't take the entire service down.
[03:18] Lena: Totally, and thank you for that transparency. High level cause chain we identified: 1) an unusual request distribution — a batch of users hitting a heavy prompt set, 2) client retry amplification, 3) runtime fallback to higher-memory model variant, 4) KV cache thrash, 5) token-throttle engaged and spilled 503s.
[03:58] Priya: Can you remind us what the token-throttle threshold is? I think our SLOs are tight—want to see how that maps to our SLA.
[04:22] Rajesh: We have per-tenant token rate and an emergency global governor. For AperturePay we were at the per-tenant cap, but the global emergency throttle kicked in when total cluster RPS crossed the safety boundary. The emergency logic is conservative by design for multi-tenant fairness, but in this case it interacted poorly with your burst pattern.
[05:05] Evan: Was there a fallback to a cheaper model that made it worse? I thought fallbacks are supposed to help.
[05:30] Rajesh: Right, normally fallbacks help. But this fallback had a different attention pattern and larger KV footprint — that increased working set and caused cache eviction churn, which then raised CPU latency on workers. So the fallback changed the cost per token dramatically in the short window.
[06:05] Marta: That rings true. We saw lower per-token latency pre-5th but our tail latency doubled during the spike.
[06:36] Noelle (checking notes): We also triggered a config change in autoscale that briefly reduced burst capacity because it misread the metric signal (we have a separate action item to tune that), so there was less headroom.
[07:05] Noah: What immediate mitigations did Redwood apply? We saw the 503s stop around 16:23.
[07:28] Lena: Good question. Timeline: once we detected the spike we engaged emergency throttles to protect overall cluster — that's what caused the 503s — then we selectively pinned affected tenants to a lower-variance model variant and scaled up worker pool with priority burst; that stabilized KV pressure and reduced the throttle.
[07:59] Daniel: The selective pinning — was that manual or automatic? We want reproducible steps.
[08:18] Rajesh: Manual in the incident — we have a canary policy framework that can do this automatically, but for this event we did a manual pin to be safe. Action: automate that pin with a safe rollback window.
[08:40] Priya: On security — there's talk internally about moving to Private deployment with KMS. Does this incident change the posture?
[09:05] Rajesh: Security posture is separate but related. Private deployment reduces surface area and gives you stronger control over network egress and KMS/HSM integration. It won't prevent client-side retry storms, but it gives you more levers — e.g., custom throttles and local cache sizing.
[09:36] Priya: And the audit logs you provide — are they sufficient for our compliance team? We saw some gaps in traceability during the incident.
[09:58] Noelle: We capture detailed request traces, token-level cost, and audit trail for config changes. I think the gap Marta mentioned is early-stage correlation between VPC flow logs and request IDs — we'll need AperturePay to share flow logs for deeper root cause.
[10:25] Marta: We'll get that. Next — is there a hardened guardrail you recommend to avoid the same cascade?
[10:42] Rajesh: Three-pronged: short term — lower client retry limits and implement jitter, mid term — auto-pin to a low-variance model when KV-miss rate crosses X%, long term — improve governor logic to degrade gracefully instead of global 503s. We'll propose concrete thresholds.
[11:17] Lena: I'll capture those thresholds with owners. Also propose a debug mode that routes a small percent of requests to a debug path with extended telemetry for a week of the pilot.
[11:35] Evan: Can you give numbers for the recommended cache sizing change? We want to know memory delta.
[11:52] Rajesh: Based on our sandboxing, bumping per-shard KV allocation from 8GB to 12GB for affected model family reduced eviction rate by ~78% for AperturePay's peak distribution. That costs roughly 2.5x the worker memory footprint for the hot partition but reduces token cost from re-computation.
[12:30] Daniel: That's significant. We need cost vs reliability analysis before we commit.
[12:45] Lena: Understood. We'll provide a TCO sheet factoring in the memory delta and one-week mitigation credits.
[13:00] Marta: Can Rajesh recap root cause in plain language for execs? We'll need a 1-paragraph summary.
[13:12] Rajesh: Sure — brief: a concentrated set of customer prompts triggered a fallback to a model variant with higher KV working set; combined with aggressive client retries and an autoscale mis-signal, this produced a cache-thrashing loop that caused global throttles and 503s.
[13:40] Noah: I noticed some transcripts refer to "kay vee cache" in our logs — the naming is inconsistent in our monitoring. Can we unify naming?
[13:54] Noelle: Yes, that's an ops hygiene item. We'll standardize metric names across instrumented stacks.
[14:10] Marta: For the remediation runbook — can we add a step for coordinated client release so you don't see a repeat when we push changes?
[14:26] Rajesh: Absolutely. We recommend phased rollouts with shadowing for two deploys and a 10% rollout window with rollback thresholds. We'll include that in the runbook.
[14:46] Priya: On KMS: you support bring-your-own-KMS, right? We are worried about keys in transit.
[15:03] Rajesh: BYO-KMS is supported in Private and Dedicated. We use envelope encryption and can integrate HSM-backed CMKs. Minor caveat: in Hosted mode we manage the key material; in Private we can bring your KMS.
[15:30] Priya: Ok send the integration checklist.
[15:38] Lena: Noted.
[15:50] Evan: Any changes needed on our SDK? We can push quicker than infra.
[16:05] Daniel: We plan to change one line — exponential backoff with capped retries, and add jitter. That's low risk.
[16:20] Rajesh: Good. If you send sample distributions of token lengths and retry behavior, we can run a replay in our test harness to show expected failure modes.
[16:40] Marta: We'll provide the distributions tonight.
[16:50] Lena: Great. Quick housekeeping — do we want a short bench next week to validate the pinning and cache bump?
[17:07] Noah: Yes, schedule it. We'll block time Tue or Wed morning PST.
[17:20] Noelle: I'll propose times.
[17:30] Rajesh: One more operational note — we'll add a safety feature: when eviction rate exceeds Y% for a tenant, auto-schedule a transient priority scale-up before global throttles. This buys time to decide on pinning vs rollbacks.
[17:52] Daniel: That sounds promising. What's the rollback plan if that scale-up creates other issues?
[18:06] Rajesh: Rollback is fast — reduce workers or re-pin to previous model; we'll codify the exact steps and guard conditions.
[18:25] Marta: From compliance view, Priya — anything else?
[18:34] Priya: Need to confirm log retention and redaction policies for private deployments. We'll review the security questionnaire you send.
[18:50] Lena: We'll attach the security doc and sample audit logs to the follow-up email.
[19:05] Evan: How do we measure success for the pilot? What's the acceptance criteria?
[19:20] Rajesh: Success: no >1% 5xxs during a 24h representative traffic window after changes, tail latency reduction to pre-incident median + <10% increase, and at least one successful coordinated client release. We'll write that into the pilot charter.
[19:48] Marta: Great. Anything else?
[19:55] Noelle: I'll summarize decisions: runbook to include 1) client retry cap/jitter, 2) auto-pin thresholds, 3) transient priority scale-up, 4) standardized metric naming, 5) scheduled bench next week.
[20:20] Lena: Perfect. Last bit — pricing for the additional worker memory and any pilot credits? I will send an offset proposal.
[20:34] Noah: We'll need that to sign off.
[20:40] Lena: Okay, we'll include numbers and a two-week pilot discount.
[20:48] Rajesh: I'll own the runbook and bench test engineering tasks.
[20:58] Marta: Thanks all, this was useful.
[21:10] Lena: Thanks team — action items and next steps in the notes. We'll reconvene after we collect the histograms and run the bench.

End of transcript.

Notes:
